title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: the preceding page reduces the problem (the excess CN−AM of a line over an arc, described by Euler as the difference between an asymptote and a hyperbola arc) to CN−AM = a√m ∫_0^1 √(1−u²)/√(1−mu²) du, with m = n²/(1+n²). This page opens with a note by N. Fuss expressing the result through Π, an arc of a conic with semiparameter 1 and semi-transverse axis a. J. A. Euler then expands the integral as a series in two ways.

Mode I. Expand (1−mu²)^{-1/2} binomially and integrate term by term. The reduction formula (λ+4)∫u^{λ+2}√(1−u²) du = (λ+1)∫u^λ√(1−u²) du − u^{λ+1}(1−u²)^{3/2} has a boundary term that vanishes on [0,1]. Starting from ∫_0^1 √(1−u²) du = π/4 it gives the moments ∫_0^1 u^{2j}√(1−u²) du = (π/4)·(1·3···(2j−1))/(4·6···(2j+2)). Hence
CN−AM = (π a√m/4)·Σ_j [(1/2)_j]² m^j /(j!(j+1)!) = (π a√m/4)·₂F₁(1/2,1/2;2;m).
In modern terms this equals a√m·(E(m) − (1−m)K(m))/m. At m=1 (n=∞) the integrand is identically 1, so CN−AM = a. This gives 1 + 1·1/(2·4) + (1·1·3·3)/(2·4·4·6) + … = 4/π, which is Gauss's summation ₂F₁(1/2,1/2;2;1) = Γ(2)/Γ(3/2)². The case m=0 gives 0 trivially.

Mode II. Put u = sinφ, so the integral becomes ∫_0^{π/2} cos²φ dφ/√(1−m sin²φ). Using cos²φ = (1+cos2φ)/2 and 1−m sin²φ = ((2−m)/2)(1+k cos2φ) with k = m/(2−m) = n²/(2+n²), this gives
CN−AM = a√(k/2) ∫_0^{π/2} (1+cos2φ)(1+k cos2φ)^{-1/2} dφ.
The binomial series in k cos2φ is then written out, together with the power-reduction formulas for cos^p 2φ as multiple-angle cosines (p = 2..5 here). On the next page only the constant terms survive integration over [0, π/2]. That yields a series in k, which converges faster than the series in m because k < m. At k=1 it gives 1 − 1/4 + 3/16 − 15/128 + … = 2√2/π. This expansion about the mean of the modulus is essentially a quadratic-transformation (Landen/Kummer-type) re-expansion of the same hypergeometric function.
errors: No mathematical errors found on this page. The checked items are: the reduction formula; the moments π/16 and π/32 for j=1,2; the m-series coefficients; the evaluation at m=1; the identity √m/√(4−2m) = √(k/2); k = n²/(2+n²); and the power formulas for cos^2–cos^5.

Fuss's closed form CN−AM = aC√m − am/(m−1)(1−u√m)Π cannot be checked from this page alone, because C and the limits are defined elsewhere. As written, the u-dependent factor looks odd for a definite integral.

ideas.what: Term-by-term binomial integration with the Wallis-type moments ∫_0^1 u^{2j}√(1−u²)du obtained by a reduction formula
ideas.modern_name: Hypergeometric series ₂F₁(1/2,1/2;2;m) for a complete elliptic integral combination (E−(1−m)K)/m
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (series for elliptic arcs, 1730s–1750s); hypergeometric framework Gauss 1812
ideas.where_published: Euler's papers on rectification of the ellipse and hyperbola (e.g. 'Animadversiones in rectificationem ellipsis'); exact location of this precise series unsure

ideas.what: Evaluation 1 + 1·1/(2·4) + 1·1·3·3/(2·4·4·6) + … = 4/π obtained from the degenerate geometric case m=1
ideas.modern_name: Gauss summation theorem special case ₂F₁(1/2,1/2;2;1) = 4/π
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss (1812) in general; such π-series via degenerate cases known to Euler
ideas.where_published: Similar π-series from degenerate ellipse/hyperbola cases appear in Euler's elliptic-arc papers

ideas.what: Substitution u=sinφ and expansion in k cos2φ about the mean value, with k = m/(2−m), using multiple-angle formulas for cos^p
ideas.modern_name: Fourier/multiple-angle expansion; equivalent to a quadratic transformation of ₂F₁ giving faster convergence
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (similar device for the ellipse perimeter, 1750); Landen/Kummer for quadratic transformations
ideas.where_published: Euler's ellipse-perimeter series papers use the same mean-modulus expansion technique

deep.surprise_reason: This is a competent but standard exercise in Euler-school series expansion of a complete elliptic integral. The resulting π-series are special cases of Gauss's summation and are well known, and nothing new or unfinished is evident.
